description: We’re building a dashboard to explore how astronauts’ health changes around a space mission. We use pre- and post-flight blood counts from NASA’s Inspiration4 study (OSD-569) and simulated heart rate and oxygen saturation to demonstrate in-flight monitoring. We’re looking for teammates with skills or interests in full-stack development, data analysis, predictive modelling, AI and API integration, UI/UX design, animation, physics, astronomy, health data categorisation, or scientific validation.
summary:
Orbit Health is a browser-based prototype that helps astronauts monitor their health during long missions. Crew members can log resting heart rate, oxygen saturation, sleep, and fatigue, track changes from their personal baselines, and record rechecks and notes. A fictional Mars transit scenario demonstrates the full workflow.

The Mission Simulator shows the same astronaut profile and latest readings alongside an interactive body map and an exposure monitor. The historical reference view charts pre- and post-flight blood measurements from NASA’s Inspiration4 study (OSD-569). It keeps those measurements separate from fictional check-ins and simulated flight conditions.

Our three-person team worked across full-stack development, data analysis, AI integration, flight simulation, and interface design. We modelled how flight conditions affect physical loads and integrated an AI assistant that helps users interpret the simulation results.
details:
Orbit Health helps astronauts log daily health indicators, spot changes from their personal baselines, and record follow-ups. To try it, load the fictional Mars transit demo, open the flagged resting heart-rate trend, log a recheck, add a note, and download the crew report. Then open Mission Simulator to see the same astronaut’s latest readings, compare conditions inside and outside the spacecraft, and select a body region to see which loads and exposure risks the simulator highlights for that region.

The app uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and is hosted on Netlify. Check-ins, notes, and simulator snapshots are saved in the browser. A Netlify Function forwards simulator questions to a Cloudflare Worker. Mission AI uses simulation outputs and NASA references to explain exposure alerts and modeled physical loads. Its answers are educational and do not predict medical outcomes.

The historical reference view charts hematocrit, platelet counts, and white blood cell counts from NASA’s Inspiration4 study, OSD-569, before and after flight. These observations appear separately from the fictional crew check-ins and modeled flight conditions. NASA’s Human Research Program hazard framework informs the simulator’s exposure explanations.

ChatGPT and Codex were used to assist with development and writing. OpenAI image generation produced the watermarked illustrations. The mission AI feature uses Groq, Gemini, and OpenRouter.
